title: Taft reception brochure and the Jonestown Wolves Club
summary: He shows a brochure from his grandfather Lewis Taylor's files about the Taft reception, and begins describing Jonestown's marching Wolves Club.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Gee, I want to get back to something. Well, we've been showing this. You showed me this thing. It's about the reception. It's a brochure.

For William Taff, when you came to the president. President William Howard Taff. You said your grandfather was involved. Yeah, my grandfather was involved with that. What was his name? His name was Taylor, Lewis Taylor. He's not in here. I was looking for him, but this came out of his files. I got a hold of this some kind of way before he died, but he was a good friend with quite a few of these people who served on the executive committee, and they got him involved. That's, you know, because I talked with him, oh, long before he died, sometime before he died, and he's always spoke politics. He lived on the west bank of the river in the area below Gretna called Jonestown. Now, why they call it Jonestown, I really don't know. But now, let me tell you about Jonestown. Jonestown had one of the largest and one of the best marching groups. They had a group over there called the Wolves Club, and it was headed at one time by a distant relative of my mother called Sidney Johnson, who just died about two years ago. He was a tall guy, about six feet, four inches tall, weighed about 235, 40 pounds. But they used to wear the arm bands like everybody else, and the hats and the dark clothes, and they used to hire bands, and they had their sashes and whatnot, and they used to party on the west bank of the river. And they, look, they were the first club in the greater metropolitan area to own their own building. They owned a hall over on the west bank of the river in Jonestown. It was called a Wolves Hall today. It was the older guys, they died.
